WINNENDEN, Germany (CNN) -- Students jumped out of windows and locked themselves in classrooms as a former pupil rampaged through a German school with a gun, killing at least a dozen people there Wednesday, a student at the school told CNN. People lay flowers at the school Wednesday. "Suddenly there were police standing in front of me and told us to run outside quickly," Luisa Santonastaso, 16, said. "At first we didn't know what to do. So first we went to the class and picked up some of our classmates and ran out. "Then we heard that someone was inside shooting. Then we also saw a teacher who had blood on his hands because he wanted to help a female teacher who sacrificed herself for a student -- she stood in front of a student to protect her," the girl told CNN by phone from Germany. "The guy just entered the classroom and started shooting and a friend of mine was panicking so much that she jumped out of a window. I think she broke her arm. She's in hospital now." Santonastaso's friend was not the only one who jumped, she said. Dressed in military gear, the gunman -- identified by police as Tim Kretschmer, 17 -- killed a total of 15 people in two different towns before he died.  Watch more about the shootings » . Initial indications are that he shot himself, but police are continuing to investigate, said Erwin Hetger, the regional chief of police. The rampage in Winnenden, a small town about 20 kilometers (12 miles) northeast of Stuttgart, and spread to neighboring Wendlingen. As people at Albertville-Realschule Winnenden school -- where Kretschmer used to be a student -- realized what was happening, many burst into tears, Santonastaso said. "Everybody was crying because nobody could really imagine what had just happened. They brought us to the swimming pool hall in Winnenden for security reasons," she said. "Then all our parents were called because no child was allowed to leave without parents," she continued. At least one parent got awful news when she arrived. "One mother came and the teachers had to tell her that her child had been injured or shot dead, and then she cried really hard and fainted," Santonastaso said. iReport.com: Town in shock over shooting . Santonastaso's own parents were more fortunate. "When I first called to tell them what had happened they wanted to come right away, but I told them that wasn't possible because we were being brought to somewhere safe," she said. Later, she said: "My parents and my friend came and we went out with them. Out there it got a bit better." CNN's Marco Woldt and Lianne Turner contributed to this report .

outputs.L2:
**WINNENDEN, Germany (CNN) —** A 16-year-old student told CNN that pupils barricaded themselves inside classrooms and escaped through windows when a former student opened fire at a German school Wednesday, killing at least 12 people on the campus. Mourners placed flowers outside the school later that day.

Luisa Santonastaso said police unexpectedly appeared and ordered students to leave immediately.

“At first, we were unsure how to react,” she said. “We went into the classroom, gathered some classmates and fled. Afterward, we learned that someone inside the building was firing a gun.”

Speaking to CNN by telephone from Germany, Santonastaso said she saw a male teacher with blood on his hands after he tried to assist a female teacher who had shielded a student with her own body.

She said the attacker walked into a classroom and began firing. One of her friends became so terrified that she leaped from a window, apparently breaking her arm. The girl was taken to a hospital. According to Santonastaso, other students also escaped by jumping from windows.

Police identified the gunman as 17-year-old Tim Kretschmer, a former student at Albertville-Realschule Winnenden. Wearing military-style clothing, he killed 15 people in total across two towns before dying himself.

Regional police chief Erwin Hetger said early evidence suggested Kretschmer had taken his own life, although the investigation remained underway.

The attack began in Winnenden, a small community approximately 20 kilometers, or 12 miles, northeast of Stuttgart, before continuing in nearby Wendlingen.

Santonastaso said many people at the school began crying once they understood what was taking place.

“No one could really comprehend what had just happened,” she said. For safety, the students were moved to a swimming-pool hall in Winnenden. Their parents were contacted, and no student was permitted to leave unless accompanied by a parent.

At least one mother received devastating information after arriving. Santonastaso said teachers told the woman that her child had either been wounded or killed. The mother cried intensely and then lost consciousness.

Santonastaso’s parents received better news. She said that when she first phoned them about the shooting, they wanted to come immediately. She explained that they could not do so because authorities were moving the students to a secure location.

Later, her parents and a friend arrived, and she was allowed to leave with them. Santonastaso said she began to feel somewhat better once she was outside.

CNN’s Marco Woldt and Lianne Turner contributed to the report.

Witnesses described scenes of panic as students fled through corridors, barricaded classroom doors and, in some cases, jumped from windows to escape. Teachers tried to protect their pupils while armed police surrounded and searched the school.

The attacker, identified as Tim Kretschmer, killed nine students and three teachers before fleeing the grounds. He later killed another person in Winnenden, seized a car and forced its driver to take him to nearby Wendlingen. There, at a car dealership, he shot and killed two more people before exchanging fire with police.

Kretschmer was wounded during the confrontation and apparently took his own life, bringing the number of people he killed to 15. Several others, including police officers, were injured during the attack and pursuit. Investigators examined how he had obtained the handgun, which came from his father’s legally owned firearms collection, and whether warning signs had been missed.

In the aftermath, grieving families, pupils and residents gathered to mourn the victims. The attack left the school community deeply traumatized and renewed debate in Germany over gun storage, school security and support for young people in psychological distress. Beyond those policy questions, the tragedy’s most enduring impact was the loss of 15 lives and the lasting suffering inflicted on survivors, relatives and an entire community.

# Teen describes chaos as gunfire erupts at German school

**WINNENDEN, Germany (CNN) —** A 16-year-old student described scenes of panic and confusion Wednesday as gunfire tore through a secondary school in southwestern Germany, forcing students to barricade classrooms before being evacuated by police.

The student, whose name was withheld because of his age, said pupils at Albertville secondary school in Winnenden initially struggled to understand what was happening. Sharp sounds echoed through the building, followed by urgent instructions to remain inside classrooms and stay away from doors and windows.

As word spread that an armed attacker was inside the school, students pushed desks against doors, turned off lights and waited in silence, he said. Police later led them from the building in groups, telling them to keep moving and not look back.

Some students emerged crying and holding hands as heavily armed officers searched the campus. Parents gathered nearby, desperately seeking information about their children.

Authorities said a 17-year-old former student entered the school Wednesday morning and opened fire, killing students and teachers. He fled the campus and later hijacked a vehicle before continuing toward Wendlingen, where more people were killed at a car dealership.

The gunman died after a shootout with police, authorities said. Fifteen victims were killed in the attacks.

Investigators identified the shooter as Tim Kretschmer and said he had used a handgun legally owned by his father. Officials were examining how he obtained the weapon and what may have motivated the rampage.

Winnenden, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) northeast of Stuttgart, was placed under tight security as emergency workers treated the wounded and investigators moved through the school.

For the 16-year-old survivor, the evacuation brought relief but little understanding of the violence that had unfolded around him. What began as an ordinary school morning ended with students being escorted past police lines into the arms of waiting families.

**Teenage gunman kills 15 in attacks at German school and car dealership**  
*Winnenden, Germany — March 12, 2009*

A 17-year-old former pupil killed 15 people in a shooting spree that began at his old school in the south-western German town of Winnenden and ended hours later in a gun battle with police in Wendlingen, about 40 kilometres away.

Police identified the gunman as Tim Kretschmer, who entered the Albertville-Realschule shortly after 9:30 a.m. on Wednesday carrying a semi-automatic pistol taken from his family home. He shot dead nine pupils—eight girls and one boy—and three female teachers before fleeing as police converged on the school.

The teenager subsequently killed an employee near a psychiatric clinic in Winnenden, investigators said. He then forced a motorist at gunpoint to drive him away from the town. The driver later escaped unharmed after a journey of roughly two hours.

Kretschmer’s flight ended in Wendlingen, where he entered a car dealership and killed a salesman and a customer. During an exchange of fire outside the premises, two police officers were wounded. The gunman was also hit and died soon afterwards from a self-inflicted gunshot, according to police.

The 15 victims, together with Kretschmer, brought the total number of dead to 16. Several other people were injured during the attacks.

### Attack began during morning lessons

Witnesses described scenes of panic at the Albertville school as shots rang out in classrooms and corridors. Pupils barricaded doors, hid under desks or escaped through windows. Teachers rushed students into locked rooms while emergency services surrounded the building.

“He simply came into the classroom and started shooting,” one pupil told German television. Others said the attacker wore dark clothing and fired without speaking.

Police said the gunman appeared to have aimed particularly at female victims during the school attack, although investigators cautioned that no motive had been established. Emergency workers treated traumatised children in nearby buildings while parents gathered outside seeking information.

Authorities initially searched the school amid fears that the attacker might still be inside. Officers later discovered that he had left the grounds before the police cordon was completed.

### Weapon taken from father’s home

Investigators said the pistol used in the killings was a Beretta 9mm weapon legally owned by Kretschmer’s father, a member of a local shooting club and licensed firearms holder. The father reportedly owned a number of guns and a large quantity of ammunition.

Most of the weapons had been secured in accordance with regulations, officials said, but the pistol used in the attack had allegedly been kept in the parents’ bedroom rather than locked in a gun safe. Prosecutors opened an investigation into how the firearm had been stored and whether the father could face criminal charges.

Police searching the family home in nearby Leutenbach found additional firearms and ammunition. Investigators were also examining Kretschmer’s computer, personal records and contacts in an effort to establish what prompted the attack.

Kretschmer had completed his studies at the Albertville-Realschule the previous year. Officials said he had not attracted attention at school as a serious disciplinary problem. Reports that he had received treatment for depression or other psychological difficulties were being investigated, but authorities had not confirmed a direct connection to the shootings.

Police also urged caution over claims that the teenager had announced the attack in an internet conversation the night before. The authenticity of an alleged online warning was disputed, and investigators said they were working to determine whether it had been fabricated.

### National mourning and renewed gun-law debate

Chancellor Angela Merkel described the killings as “an appalling crime” and said Germany was united in grief with the victims’ families.

“It is unimaginable that in just seconds pupils and teachers were killed,” Merkel said. “This is a day of mourning for the whole of Germany.”

President Horst Köhler and political leaders across the country expressed their condolences. Flags were lowered, church services were held and residents placed flowers and candles near the sealed school grounds.

The attack immediately renewed debate over Germany’s gun laws, which were tightened after a 19-year-old former pupil killed 16 people and himself at a school in Erfurt in 2002. German law generally requires firearms owners to be licensed and to keep guns and ammunition securely stored, but critics said the Winnenden killings showed that enforcement and household inspections needed to be strengthened.

Officials also faced questions about school security, the availability of mental-health support for adolescents and the influence of violent media. Authorities warned, however, against drawing conclusions before the investigation had established Kretschmer’s motives and preparations.

Classes at the Albertville-Realschule were suspended as police completed forensic work. Counsellors and psychologists were sent to support surviving pupils, teachers, emergency personnel and bereaved families.

For Winnenden, a community of about 27,000 people near Stuttgart, the attack was an unprecedented tragedy. Residents gathered silently outside churches and public buildings as the names of the victims began to emerge, while police continued reconstructing the gunman’s movements from the school to the final confrontation in Wendlingen.
